```{r}

df<- read.csv("thermometers_hw04.csv")
df <- df %>%
  filter(!is.na(ft_immig) & ft_immig != "") %>%
  filter(!is.na(ft_dem) & ft_dem != "")


```

# 1.a

```{r}
#recoding ft_immig column --> *do not change into factor! then you can't run the regression
df$ft_immig[df$ft_immig%in% 0:19]<-1
df$ft_immig[df$ft_immig%in% 20:39]<-2
df$ft_immig[df$ft_immig%in%40:59]<-3
df$ft_immig[df$ft_immig%in% 60:79]<-4
df$ft_immig[df$ft_immig%in%80:100]<-5

#checking new values
table(df$ft_immig)


im_dem_model<- lm(ft_immig~ft_dem, data=df)
summary(im_dem_model)
```

A one unit increase on the feeling thermometer for democrats is associated with a 0.016 unit higher expected value of the warmth feeling thermometer for immigrants.

# 1.b

```{r}

df<-df %>%
  mutate(two=ifelse(ft_immig>=2 ,1,0))%>%
  mutate(three= ifelse(ft_immig>=3,1,0))%>%
  mutate(four=ifelse(ft_immig>=4,1,0))%>%
  mutate(five=ifelse( ft_immig>= 5,1,0))
  
b_model_two<-lm(two~ft_dem,data=df)
b_model_three<-lm(three~ft_dem,data=df)
b_model_four<-lm(four~ft_dem,data=df)
b_model_five<-lm(five~ft_dem,data=df)

summary(b_model_two)
summary(b_model_three)
summary(b_model_four)
summary(b_model_five)

#adding together all slopes to ensure they are the same as the lm model run in part (a)
0.0047892+0.0057298+0.0033948+0.0020987
```

Slope when variable is 2: 0.002\
Slope when variable is 3: 0.003\
Slope when variable is 4: 0.006 (0.0057)\
Slope when variable is 5: 0.005 (0.0047)\
\
Each of the slopes are different.\
The greatest probability of moving up a category is when the variable is 4 or greater but when the variable is 5 or greater the slope decreases slightly.\
\
Adding up all the slopes:\
0.0047892+0.0057298+0.0033948+0.0020987 = 0.0160125\
When added all together, the four slopes equal the slope found in part (a), which included all categorical variables 1-5.

# 1.c

```{r}
im_dem_model
residuals<-resid(im_dem_model)
fitted<-fitted(im_dem_model)

a<- ggplot(df,aes(x=fitted, y= residuals))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_hline(yintercept=0, linetype="dashed", color="red")+
  labs(x= "Fitted Values", y= "Residuals",
       title= " Residuals vs Fitted Values")

# residual vs fitted plot for k=3
residuals.b<-resid(b_model_three)
fitted.b<-fitted(b_model_three)
b<-ggplot(df,aes(x=fitted.b, y= residuals.b))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_hline(yintercept=0, linetype="dashed", color="orange")+
  labs(x= "Fitted Values", y= "Residuals",
       title= " Residuals vs Fitted Values: k=3")

a+b
```

The errors are not constant. They create lines in the graph; which represent each categorical variable. For the plot representing k=3, the variable used in the lm model only has two outcomes: 1 or 0. Thus, there are only two bands represented in the plot.

# 1.d

```{r}
#resetting the ft_immig numbers back to thermometer. 

df<- read.csv("thermometers_hw04.csv")
df <- df %>%
  filter(!is.na(ft_immig) & ft_immig != "") %>%
  filter(!is.na(ft_dem) & ft_dem != "")


k<- c(3,5,10,50,100) #creating k 
results<- data.frame(k= integer(), slopecat_converted=numeric(), r2of.cat= numeric(),slope_t=numeric(), r2.t=numeric()) #empty vector to store loop results. 


for(k in k){
  ft.immig_cat<-cut(df$ft_immig,
         breaks=seq(min(df$ft_immig),max(df$ft_immig),length.out= k+1),labels= FALSE, include.lowest = TRUE) #creating cutoff points k
  
  model.ftimmig.cat<- lm (ft.immig_cat~ ft_dem, data=df) #creating a lm model using the categorical version of ft_immig
  
  slopeof.cat<- coef(model.ftimmig.cat)["ft_dem"] # slope of categorical ft_immig
  r2of.cat<- summary(model.ftimmig.cat)$r.squared
  
  slopecat_converted<- (slopeof.cat*100)/k #converting slope from categorical back to thermom. scale. 

  #original thermometer regression to compare k slope values against 
model.t<-lm(ft_immig~ft_dem, data=df)
slope_t<- coef(model.t)["ft_dem"]
r2.t<- summary(model.t)$r.squared

results<- rbind(results, data.frame(k=k, 
                                    slopecat_converted=slopecat_converted, 
                                    r2of.cat=r2of.cat,
                                    slope_t=slope_t,
                                    r2.t=r2.t))

         
}

print(results)


```

As K increases the categorical slope and r2 (slopecat_converted & r2.cat) grows similar to the original thermometer slope and r2 score (slope_t & r2.t).\
Thus, the more categories you have the more accurate your regression coefficients will be.
